opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I use them constantly, probably more than I'd like to admit. A big part of my work is evaluations: figuring out how capable models are on real-world, economically valuable tasks. So I'm in this funny position where I'm both measuring the models and relying on them all day.

Day to day, I use them a lot for coding. Spinning up analysis scripts, debugging, cleaning data, that kind of thing. They've gotten good enough that I often treat them like a collaborator. I'll describe what I'm trying to do, let the model take a first pass, and then iterate. I also use them for writing, for drafting docs and tightening my thinking, and as a sounding board when I'm designing an eval. I'll ask things like, "What would a domain expert say is missing from this task?" or "How might a model game this grader?"

What's interesting is that working on evals changes how you use the models. You develop a pretty calibrated sense of where they're strong and where they still fall short. So I try to give them tasks where I can quickly verify the output, and I stay skeptical in areas where I know they tend to be confidently wrong. But the frontier keeps moving. Things I wouldn't have trusted a model with six months ago, I now hand off without thinking twice. That shift is a big part of why I think measuring this carefully matters so much.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it uses models often for coding, writing, and eval design, and lets them take a first pass in those workflows. It does not say this happens for essentially every work task.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes using its evaluation experience to judge model strengths and weaknesses, but does not say it turns everyday instances of inadequate performance into evaluation cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I use models constantly, and I've noticed my habits have shifted a lot over the past year or so. It used to be that I'd mostly reach for a model when I had a specific, bounded question, like "help me debug this," or "rewrite this paragraph." Now it's much more like having a collaborator sitting next to me throughout the day.

A big part of my job is thinking about evaluations, so a lot of my model use is actually me poking at the models to understand where they're strong and where they fall over. But in the course of that, you learn to use them well for real work. I'll have a model draft the scaffolding of an analysis, write the boring parts of code, summarize a long thread I missed, or stress-test an argument I'm making. I like asking it to argue against me, actually. If I have a take on why some eval design is right, I'll ask the model to give me the strongest case that it's wrong, and surprisingly often it finds something I hadn't considered.

The other thing I'd say is that I've gotten more comfortable giving the model longer, more open-ended tasks and letting it run. The agentic stuff has gotten genuinely useful. I'll describe what I want at a fairly high level, let it go, and then review the result rather than babysitting every step. That's a different muscle. You have to learn what to delegate and how to verify the output, because the failure modes are subtle. It'll produce something that looks polished and confident, and you still have to check it.

So I guess my approach is: use it a lot, be curious about its limits, and never fully outsource your judgment.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes frequent, varied model use, but does not say they give the model a first pass at essentially every work task.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses probing model strengths and weaknesses for evaluation work, but does not describe turning inadequate everyday performance into evaluation cases.

astra-6.text: I tend to start with a task I’m already trying to get done and ask where a model could help me make progress. Sometimes that’s brainstorming, sometimes it’s working through a technical question, and sometimes it’s getting a first draft down so I have something to react to. I think the most useful habit is to iterate: give it context, look critically at what comes back, and refine the question. I still need to exercise judgment, but it can make that process much faster.

r001.rationale: The response says models can help with some tasks, but does not describe giving a model a first pass at essentially every work task.

r002.rationale: The response mentions reviewing and refining model output, but does not describe turning inadequate performance into evaluation cases.

sol-6.1.text: I tend to start with the task rather than the model. What am I trying to get done, and where would another perspective help? Sometimes that means using AI to brainstorm, sometimes to work through a problem, and sometimes to critique something I’ve already written. I like making it an iterative conversation: give it context, look at what comes back, and refine from there. And I still check the details and use my own judgment about the final result.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing AI based on the task and says it can help in some situations; it does not say the model takes a first pass at essentially every work task.

r002.rationale: The response mentions checking details and using personal judgment, but does not describe turning inadequate model performance into evaluation cases.
